turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome. What brings you into the clinic today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, my wife is the one who wanted me to come in. She works over in the administration building—they actually just finished renovating the east wing over there. Took them eighteen months, which is completely ridiculous. When I was finishing my graduate degree, they built the entire library annex in under a year. The contractors they hire nowadays just drag their feet to bill more hours. I mentioned that to the professor I assist for, but, you know, nobody really listens to the teaching assistants. 

But anyway, she wanted me to talk to someone because... well, I know she says the late meetings and these little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff. She uses that new messaging app for her team. I told her she should use something more secure, honestly. My brother had his identity stolen a few years ago, and it took him nearly six months just to fix his credit score. It's an absolute nightmare when your information gets out there like that. 

But... for the past year, her schedule and the way those messages are worded, they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental. It’s like there’s a private signal in them, meant to tell me something she just won’t say directly.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, referential belief that his wife's normal work messages and schedule contain hidden, private signals directed at him.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech is highly tangential, frequently drifting into unrelated topics like building renovations, contractors, and his brother's identity theft before returning to the main point.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from noticing these messages, have you ever heard any voices or sounds that other people couldn't hear?
turns.patient_response: No, no, nothing like that. I don't hear things that aren't there. My hearing is actually perfectly fine, though I did have this awful ear infection back in my twenties. I was swimming a lot at the university pool—this old indoor one with the terrible ventilation, you know? The chlorine smell would just hang in the air, and it ruined two of my favorite swim caps. Anyway, the doctor gave me these drops that burned like crazy, but my hearing has been sharp ever since. I can hear the neighbor's dog barking from three houses down, which is a whole other issue because they leave him out all night. I've thought about calling the city, but you know how local government is, you fill out a form and it just goes into a black hole. But no, I don't hear voices or anything. It's just the messages, the way they're written.

turns.doctor_question: What do you believe she is trying to secretly tell you through those messages?
turns.patient_response:
Well, that's the frustrating part, I... I really don't know exactly what she's trying to say. If I knew, I wouldn't be so stressed about it, right? It's just the pattern of it that stands out. Patterns are funny like that. I was actually grading these introductory statistics papers last week for the professor I work with, and you wouldn't believe how terrible the undergrads are at recognizing basic data trends. I mean, they just plug numbers into the software without even looking at the scatter plots to see if it makes sense. 

When I took stats back in the late nineties, my professor made us do the calculations by hand for the first month. He was this older guy, always wore these horrible heavy tweed jackets with the leather elbow patches. Just a walking cliché, you know? But he really knew his stuff. I think he retired to Florida a few years back. Or maybe it was Arizona? Somewhere hot. My wife actually hates the heat. We went to Phoenix once for an academic conference and she complained about the dry air the entire time. We ended up spending most of the trip inside the hotel lobby. 

But anyway, yeah, I don't know what the actual secret is in the messages. I just know they aren't normal office chatter. It's like... I know there's a signal there, I just don't have the key to decipher what she wants me to know.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient maintains a fixed belief that there are secret signals hidden in his wife's messages, demonstrating a delusion.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality, wandering off-topic from the secret messages to grading statistics papers, his old professor, and a trip to Phoenix before finally returning to the question.

No, no, I don't have any kind of... special powers or a sixth sense or anything like that. I'm a very logical person. I deal with data and facts. Which is why this whole thing is so maddening. It's not magic, it's just... observation. 

Speaking of observation, I was watching this documentary the other night about how magicians use misdirection. It's actually fascinating how they manipulate your attention. They had this guy on there who used to perform in Vegas in the eighties, and he was explaining how the brain just fills in the gaps when it doesn't have all the information. Vegas is such a strange place, honestly. I went there for a bachelor party years ago for my cousin Mark. Mark's an accountant now, lives in Chicago. He married this woman who makes these incredible ceramic bowls, just really beautiful glaze work. We have one sitting on our dining room table right now. I usually keep my keys in it, but I had to move them because the metal was scratching the bottom. 

But no, I'm not clairvoyant. I don't read minds. I just read the messages, and I can see that they aren't what they pretend to be. I just... I just don't know what they actually are.

turns.patient_response:
Do I think people are generally untrustworthy? No, not at all. Most people are pretty straightforward, I think. I don't go around suspecting everyone is up to something. 

Like, I trust my students, for the most part. Whenever they ask for an extension on an assignment, I usually give it to them without asking for proof. Life happens, right? Just last semester, I had this one student—a sophomore, I think—who said his laptop crashed right in the middle of writing his midterm essay. It happens. I actually had a hard drive fail on me back in 2012 and lost a whole section of my research. I had to pay this data recovery place downtown to salvage it. They were located right next to this fantastic little Thai restaurant, the one with the really good Pad Kee Mao. They use actual fresh holy basil, which makes such a huge difference compared to the dried stuff. I used to go there every Tuesday for lunch until they raised their prices. It’s really a shame how expensive eating out has gotten lately. You can barely get a decent lunch for under fifteen dollars now. 

But anyway, yeah, I gave the kid an extra three days to turn in his paper. I don't assume everyone is lying to me or has some hidden agenda. It's really just... those specific messages from her. That's the only thing in my life that feels like a puzzle I'm supposed to figure out. Everything else is just normal.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient reiterates a fixed belief that specific messages from a woman are a puzzle they are supposed to figure out, indicating a delusion.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from a story about a student to a hard drive failure, a Thai restaurant, and the price of eating out before returning to the point.
symptom_reasoning.S072: The patient explicitly denies having pervasive negative beliefs about others, stating they do not think people are generally untrustworthy or lying.

I had to rip up the oak planks—which was a shame, because they were original to the house, this beautiful quartersawn white oak. You just don't see grain patterns like that in modern lumber anymore. Everything now is just fast-grown pine, no character to it at all. I spent two weekends going to architectural salvage yards trying to find replacement boards that would match the patina. I finally found some at this place out by the old rail yards. The guy who runs it is a real character, he wears these suspenders and always has a cigar unlit in his mouth. He told me he pulled the boards out of an old textile mill that was being demolished. It makes you wonder, you know? About all the people who walked on those floors before. All those workers, day in and day out, running the looms. The noise must have been deafening. I read once that textile workers often went partially deaf by the time they were thirty because of the machinery.
